title: Trijata's comfort
hookLine: Ravana flies Sita over the battlefield to break her, and a rakshasi from his own house reads the signs
carry: dharma lives in deeds, not in birth

cards: Indrajit reports to his father: they're dead. Ravana is delighted, and he thinks of Sita. If she sees them lying there, she'll stop hoping, and she'll be his.
So he has her put in the Pushpaka, the flying chariot, and flown out over the battlefield.
Below her, among the shattered monkey army, she sees them: Rama and Lakshmana on the ground, bound and still, pierced all over with arrows. And she breaks down.

teach.b: Sita's lament in Valmiki is raw.
She recalls the signs read on her body as a girl, promising she'd never be a widow, and calls them all lies.
Beside her in the chariot is Trijata, a rakshasi, one of her guards from the ashoka grove, who had dreamed of Ravana's fall and told the others to leave Sita alone.
Her comfort now is careful, almost like evidence in a trial. Look at their faces, she says. The faces of the dead lose their color; theirs haven't.

Look at the army: if the leader were dead, they'd be scattered and running. Instead they're gathered around him, guarding him. And the last sign: this Pushpaka would not carry you if you were a widow.
They're alive. So Sita is flown back to the grove, still afraid, but holding on.
Down on the field, Rama wakes first. The serpents still hold him, but his grief is all for his brother, and he tells Sugriva to take the army home. Now look at who is good in this war, and who isn't.
Ravana is the grandson of a great sage, Pulastya, and learned in the Vedas.
The ones choosing truth and kindness are Vibhishana, who crossed the sea, and Trijata, a rakshasi from Ravana's own household, beside a weeping prisoner.

teach.h: DHARMA LIVES IN DEEDS, NOT BIRTH.
teach.b: Many teachers read the Ramayana this way: dharma isn't something you're born into; it's what you choose to do. Ravana sent Sita up to lose hope, and someone from his own house sent her down with some.
Worth remembering at school or at work, when someone from the other side is the one who tells you the truth, kindly.

how: Ramayana tellers remember Trijata as Sita's friend in Lanka, and often linger on her comfort over the battlefield.

o: the serpent-arrows Ravana uses to try to break Sita's hope
the arrows Rama shoots back blindly into the clouds
the arrows Sita's guards would fire if she ran

games.q: over the battlefield — tap the pairs.
p: wakes first and grieves for Lakshmana

s: Ravana flies Sita over the field to comfort her
he wants her to see them fallen and give up hope.
Trijata is one of Sita's rakshasi guards
she had dreamed of Ravana's fall and told the others to leave Sita alone.
Ravana came from a line of sages
he was a grandson of the sage Pulastya, and learned, yet he chose wrong.

games.q: someone from the crowd that mocked you last year sticks up for you today. your friend says 'she's one of THEM.' by the Ramayana, what fits?
o: judge her by what she did: Trijata and Vibhishana came from Ravana's own house.
keep your distance; people never really change sides.
trust her with everything now; one good day settles it.
games.why: Trijata, a rakshasi guard, comforted Sita; Ravana, a sage's grandson, held her captive. in the Ramayana, dharma is what you do.

practice: Picture someone you know who is frightened right now. Like Trijata, look for one true sign of hope you could point to for them. Fold your hands and hold it up as a small prayer for them, with each slow breath.
If you don't pray, simply hold it for them, gently.

wordCard.voice: Indrajit's arrows. They brought Rama and Lakshmana down, and Ravana tried to use the sight of it to break Sita. A rakshasi from his own house held her up.

orig.note: Sanskrit Trijaṭā: 'three braids', from tri, three, and jaṭā, braided or matted hair.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma lives in deeds, not in birth. Help is coming, out of the sky. Until tomorrow.
